content: The usual dosage range for erythromycin base is 250-500 mg orally every 6-12 hours, or 500 mg every 12 hours, or 333 mg orally every 8 hours. For severe infections, the dosage can be increased up to 4 grams per day. It is recommended to take erythromycin on an empty stomach if possible, although the PCE Dispertab formulation may be taken with food. The base form of erythromycin has the poorest absorption. For specific conditions, the following regimens are used: 1-4 grams per day orally in divided doses for 21 days. 500 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days. 1 gram orally at 1:00 PM, 2:00 PM, and 11:00 PM on the day before surgery, in combination with oral neomycin and mechanical cleansing of the large intestine. 500 mg orally every 6 hours for 21 days. 500 mg orally every 6 hours for 14 days. 250-500 mg orally three times daily before meals. 500 mg orally four times daily for 21 days. 500 mg orally three times daily for 7 days. For mild to moderate infections, the dosage is 30-50 mg/kg/day orally, divided every 6-12 hours, not exceeding 2 grams per day. For severe infections, the dosage is 15-50 mg/kg/day orally, not exceeding 4 grams per day. Specific pediatric regimens include: 50 mg/kg/day orally divided every 6 hours for 14 days. 40-50 mg/kg/day orally divided every 6 hours for 14 days, not exceeding 2 grams per day. 20 mg/kg/day orally divided every 12 hours. 20 mg/kg orally at 1:00 PM, 2:00 PM, and 11:00 PM on the day before surgery, in combination with oral neomycin and mechanical cleansing of the large intestine. Erythromycin base interacts with numerous drugs, often leading to increased levels or effects of the co-administered drug due to inhibition of hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. These interactions can result in significant clinical consequences, including QT interval prolongation, increased risk of torsades de pointes, and other serious arrhythmias. In many cases, co-administration is contraindicated or requires careful monitoring and dose adjustments. Below are specific interactions: 1. Arsenic trioxide: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. Co-administration is contraindicated. 2. Dihydroergotamine: Erythromycin increases its levels via CYP3A4 inhibition. Co-administration is contraindicated. 3. Disopyramide: Both drugs increase the QTc interval. Co-administration is contraindicated. 4. Fluconazole: Increases erythromycin levels and both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration is contraindicated. 5. Simvastatin and Lovastatin: Erythromycin increases their levels, raising the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Co-administration is contraindicated. 6. Amiodarone: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs used. 7. Citalopram: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs used. 8. Clopidogrel: Erythromycin reduces its bioactivation by inhibiting CYP3A4. Co-administration should be avoided. 9. Clozapine: Erythromycin increases its levels and both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided. 10. Chlorpromazine: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided. 11. Carbamazepine: Erythromycin increases its levels, while carbamazepine decreases erythromycin levels. Plasma levels should be monitored if co-administered. 12. Amitriptyline: Erythromycin increases its levels and both prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided. 13. Buprenorphine: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided. 14. Atorvastatin: Erythromycin increases its levels, raising the risk of myopathy. Co-administration should be avoided. 15. Cimetidine: Increases erythromycin levels via CYP3A4 inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 16. Clarithromycin: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration should be avoided. 17. Cilostazol: Erythromycin increases its levels. Dose reduction of cilostazol should be considered. 18. Aprepitant: Both drugs increase each other’s levels via CYP3A4 inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 19. Bosutinib: Erythromycin increases its levels via CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 20. Budesonide: Erythromycin increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided. In cases where co-administration is unavoidable, close monitoring, dose adjustments, or alternative therapies should be considered. For drugs that prolong the QTc interval, ECG monitoring is recommended to mitigate the risk of arrhythmias.
